question: What's actually the difference between a container and a virtual machine?
answer_html:
A virtual machine virtualizes hardware. A hypervisor sits on the host and carves out virtual CPUs, memory, and disk for each VM, and each VM boots its own full operating system, including its own kernel. That's why VMs are heavyweight: you're paying the cost of an entire OS (memory footprint, boot time, patching) per VM.

A container virtualizes at the operating system level instead. All containers on a host share the same host kernel, and isolation between them is provided by kernel features rather than a hypervisor, mainly namespaces (what a process can see) and cgroups (how much it can use). A container is really just a regular process on the host, started with a restricted view of the filesystem, network, and process table.

  • Startup time: containers start in milliseconds because there's no OS to boot; VMs take seconds to minutes.
  • Overhead: containers only carry the app and its dependencies, not a full guest OS, so they're much lighter on disk and memory.
  • Isolation strength: a VM's isolation boundary is the hypervisor and a separate kernel, which is stronger; a container's boundary is the host kernel itself, so a kernel-level exploit can, in principle, affect every container on that host.

In short: VMs isolate hardware and run many kernels on one machine; containers isolate processes and share one kernel across many workloads.

question: What's the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
answer_html:
A Docker image is a read-only template: a packaged filesystem plus metadata (what command to run, what ports to expose, what environment variables to set). It's built once, from a Dockerfile, and doesn't change after it's built.

A Docker container is a running instance of an image. When you run docker run myimage, Docker takes the image's read-only layers and adds a thin writable layer on top, then starts the process defined in the image inside its own isolated namespaces. Any files the process creates or modifies live in that writable layer.

A useful analogy: an image is like a class or a program on disk, and a container is like an object instance or a running process. You can start many containers from the same image, each with its own writable layer and its own isolated state, and they won't interfere with each other or with the original image.

question: What is a Dockerfile, and what do instructions like FROM, RUN, COPY, and CMD actually do?
answer_html:
A Dockerfile is a plain-text file containing a sequence of instructions that docker build reads from top to bottom to produce an image. Each instruction typically produces a new filesystem layer on top of the previous one.

  • FROM picks the base image everything else builds on top of, for example FROM node:20-slim.
  • RUN executes a command at build time inside the image being built (e.g. installing packages) and commits the resulting filesystem change as a new layer.
  • COPY (and its cousin ADD) copies files from the build context on your machine into the image's filesystem.
  • CMD (or ENTRYPOINT) doesn't run at build time at all — it just records the default command that should be executed when a container starts from this image.

The key distinction to keep straight: RUN shapes what ends up baked into the image, while CMD/ENTRYPOINT only decides what process starts when someone later runs a container from it.

question: How do image layers and the union filesystem actually work?
answer_html:
Almost every instruction in a Dockerfile produces a new layer: essentially a diff describing what files were added, changed, or removed relative to the layer below it. An image is really just an ordered stack of these layers plus some metadata, and each layer is content-addressed (identified by a hash of its contents), which is why Docker can reuse identical layers across different images.

Docker uses a union filesystem (commonly the overlay2 storage driver on Linux) to present that stack of separate layers to a process as one single, coherent filesystem. The layers are read-only; when a container runs, Docker adds one more layer on top that is writable, and that's the only layer that ever changes for that specific container.

This is also where copy-on-write comes in: if a running container modifies a file that physically lives in one of the read-only image layers below it, the union filesystem first copies that file up into the container's writable layer, then applies the change there. The original image layers, and any other container sharing them, are never touched.

Because layers are content-addressed and shareable, two images built from the same base image only store that base image's layers once on disk, not once per image — this is a big part of why Docker is disk- and network-efficient.

question: How does Docker's build cache work, and how should you order a Dockerfile to take advantage of it?
answer_html:
When you run docker build, Docker evaluates each instruction and checks whether it already has a cached layer for that exact instruction, given the exact state of everything above it. If nothing changed — the instruction text and the relevant input files are identical to a previous build — Docker reuses the existing layer instead of re-executing it. As soon as one instruction's cache is invalidated, every instruction after it is invalidated too and must be re-run, even if their outcome would have been identical.

This makes instruction order matter a lot. The rule of thumb is: put things that change rarely near the top, and things that change often near the bottom.

  • Base image and system-level setup first (FROM, OS packages) — these almost never change.
  • Dependency manifests and installs next — for example, COPY package.json . then RUN npm install, or COPY requirements.txt . then RUN pip install -r requirements.txt.
  • Application source code last — COPY . . — since this changes on every commit.

With that ordering, editing a source file only invalidates the final COPY layer; the expensive dependency-install layer above it stays cached and the build finishes in seconds instead of minutes. If you instead copy all the source code before installing dependencies, any code change forces a full reinstall on every build.

question: What is a multi-stage build, and why would you use one?
answer_html:
A multi-stage build is a Dockerfile with more than one FROM instruction, where each FROM starts a new, independent build stage. You can name a stage with AS (e.g. FROM golang:1.22 AS builder) and then, from a later stage, copy specific files out of an earlier one with COPY --from=builder /app/bin /usr/local/bin/app.

The typical use case: your build stage installs compilers, build tools, dev dependencies, and the full source tree to produce a compiled binary or bundled artifact. None of that is needed to actually run the application. The final stage starts fresh from a small runtime base image and copies over only the compiled output, leaving the compilers, source code, caches, and dev dependencies behind in the discarded build stage.

The result is a much smaller final image, and importantly, a smaller attack surface — there's no compiler toolchain, package manager cache, or source code sitting in the image that ships to production. It also means you no longer need a separate CI step to clean up build artifacts; the multi-stage boundary does that for you automatically.

question: What's the difference between a Docker volume and a bind mount, and when would you use each?
answer_html:
Both are ways to give a container access to data that lives outside its writable layer and therefore survives even if the container is removed. The difference is who manages the storage location.

A bind mount maps a specific, existing path on the host filesystem directly into the container, e.g. -v /home/user/app:/app. You own that path; Docker just makes it visible inside the container. Because it points at a real host directory, it's ideal for local development — you can edit source files on your host and see the change immediately inside the running container, useful for hot-reload workflows.

A volume is storage that Docker itself creates and manages (by default under its own storage area, e.g. /var/lib/docker/volumes on Linux). You reference it by name, e.g. -v mydata:/var/lib/postgresql/data, and don't need to know or care where it physically lives. Because Docker owns the lifecycle, volumes are more portable across hosts, easier to back up, and don't depend on a particular host directory layout existing.

Rule of thumb: use volumes for persistent application data you want Docker to manage, like a database's data directory. Use bind mounts when you specifically need to expose an existing host path, like syncing local source code into a dev container or mounting a host config file.

question: What are the main Docker networking modes, and when would you use each?
answer_html:
bridge is the default mode for standalone containers. Docker creates a private internal network on the host; each container gets its own IP on that network and reaches the outside world through NAT. To let something outside the host reach the container, you have to explicitly publish a port, e.g. -p 8080:80. This is the right default for most single-host, multi-container setups.

host removes the network isolation entirely: the container shares the host's network namespace directly, so a process listening on port 80 inside the container is listening on port 80 of the host itself, no NAT and no -p mapping needed. It's faster (no NAT overhead) but sacrifices isolation, and you have to manage port conflicts yourself since the container's ports and the host's ports are the same ports.

overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts, typically in a Swarm cluster. They let containers running on different physical or virtual machines discover and talk to each other as if they were on the same local network, which is what makes multi-host container orchestration practical.

none gives the container no network interface at all beyond loopback. It's used when a workload genuinely has no need for network access, which minimizes what an attacker could do if that container were compromised.

question: What problem does Docker Compose solve, and what is it good for?
answer_html:
Docker Compose lets you describe a multi-container application — its services, the networks connecting them, and the volumes they use — in a single YAML file (docker-compose.yml), and then bring the whole thing up or down with one command, docker compose up / docker compose down.

Without Compose, running a multi-service app (say, an API, a database, and a cache) means manually creating a network, then running each container with the right flags, in the right order, with the right environment variables — and remembering to repeat all of that identically every time. Compose captures that setup as code.

  • It automatically creates a shared network for the project and registers each service's name as a DNS hostname on it, so the api service can simply connect to db:5432 instead of tracking IP addresses.
  • depends_on lets you express startup ordering between services.
  • Environment variables, volumes, and port mappings are all declared once, in version control, instead of typed manually.

Compose is primarily a local development and small-deployment tool, running on a single Docker host. It is not a substitute for a production orchestrator like Swarm or Kubernetes, which add things Compose doesn't: scheduling across many hosts, self-healing/rescheduling failed containers, and rolling updates across a cluster.

question: What Linux kernel primitives does Docker actually rely on to isolate containers?
answer_html:
Two separate kernel mechanisms do the work, and it's worth keeping them conceptually distinct: one controls what a process can see, the other controls how much it can use.

Namespaces give a process its own isolated view of a particular kind of system resource. Docker puts each container in its own set of namespaces, including: pid (the container sees only its own process tree, so its main process can be PID 1 inside the container even though it's some ordinary PID on the host), net (its own network interfaces, IP addresses, and routing table), mnt (its own filesystem mount points), uts (its own hostname), ipc (isolated inter-process communication resources like shared memory), and user (the ability to map container UIDs/GIDs to different, typically unprivileged, UIDs/GIDs on the host).

cgroups (control groups) do the opposite job: they don't hide resources, they meter and cap them. Flags like --memory and --cpus on docker run translate directly into cgroup limits, so a single container can be prevented from consuming all of the host's RAM or CPU and starving its neighbors.

The important thing this implies: containers on the same host all share one kernel. Namespaces and cgroups are enforced by that shared kernel, so a vulnerability in the kernel itself can potentially be exploited to break out of a container's isolation — this is the fundamental way container isolation is weaker than a VM's, which runs an entirely separate kernel under a hypervisor.

question: What would you actually do to harden a Docker image and its runtime configuration for production?
answer_html:
Run as a non-root user. By default, if you don't specify otherwise, a container's process runs as root inside the container. Add a dedicated user in the Dockerfile and switch to it with USER appuser before the final CMD. This limits what an attacker can do if the application process is ever compromised — they don't automatically get root-level access within the container's filesystem and capabilities.

Use minimal base images. Slim, Alpine, or distroless variants ship far fewer packages than a full OS image, which means a smaller attack surface, fewer known CVEs to track, and faster pulls. This pairs naturally with multi-stage builds, since the final stage only needs a runtime, not a full build toolchain.

Scan images for known vulnerabilities. Tools like Trivy, Docker Scout, Snyk, or a registry's built-in scanning (e.g. Amazon ECR image scanning) check your base image and installed packages against CVE databases. Running this in CI, before an image is pushed or deployed, catches known-vulnerable dependencies early instead of finding out in an audit.

Handle secrets correctly. Never bake credentials into the image with ENV, ARG, or by COPY-ing a secrets file — anything written into a layer persists in the image and its history, and can be extracted with docker history or by inspecting the layers, even if a later layer deletes the file. Instead, inject secrets at runtime through environment variables, mounted files, or an orchestrator's native secret mechanism (Kubernetes Secrets, Docker Swarm secrets, AWS Secrets Manager), and for build-time-only secrets use BuildKit's --mount=type=secret, which exposes the value to a single RUN step without ever committing it to a layer.

  • Drop unneeded Linux capabilities (--cap-drop ALL, then add back only what's required) instead of running fully privileged.
  • Pin image tags to specific versions or digests rather than :latest, so a rebuild doesn't silently pull in a different base image.
  • Consider a read-only root filesystem (--read-only) for processes that don't need to write outside specific mounted paths.

question: How would you debug a container that exits immediately after starting, versus one that runs fine under normal load but misbehaves under heavy load?
answer_html:
Container exits immediately: start with docker logs <container> to see anything the application printed before it stopped, and docker inspect <container> (or docker ps -a) to check the exit code. Exit code 0 usually means the container's main process simply finished and returned — a very common cause is that CMD/ENTRYPOINT runs a script that isn't actually a long-running foreground process (a container stops as soon as its PID 1 process exits, by design). Exit code 137 typically means the process was killed, often by the kernel's out-of-memory killer. Any other non-zero code usually means the application itself crashed on startup — check the logs for a stack trace. A useful technique is to override the entrypoint and get a shell instead, e.g. docker run -it --entrypoint sh myimage, to poke around the filesystem and try running the intended command manually to see the real error.

Misbehaving or dying under heavy load: first rule out resource exhaustion. docker stats shows live CPU/memory usage per container; if memory climbs to the container's limit and it dies with exit code 137, confirm an OOM kill specifically with docker inspect --format='{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <container> or by checking dmesg on the host for OOM killer log entries. If there's a CPU limit set (--cpus), the container won't be killed for exceeding it, but it will be throttled by the CPU cgroup, which shows up as increased latency rather than crashes — worth ruling out if the symptom is slow rather than dead. Beyond infra-level limits, check the application itself: connection pool sizes, file descriptor limits, and whether it's blocking on a single thread while load piles up. docker exec -it <container> sh lets you attach to a live container and inspect processes and open connections in place.

In both cases, the general approach is the same: get the exit code and logs first, confirm or rule out resource limits second, and only then start guessing at application-level causes.
